lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 4, what did the Shang kings of China use to ask questions of their ancestors? (Oracle bones.) Much later, in 206 BC, the Han dynasty began. It ruled China for over 400 years.

The first Han emperor, Liu Bang, was born a farmer's son. Han emperors ran a huge land through trained officials who studied the teachings of Confucius: respect your family, work hard, and rule kindly and fairly. Many Chinese people still call themselves Han.

Before paper, the Chinese wrote on strips of bamboo and on silk. Early paper was made in Han times. In AD 105 an official, Cai Lun, showed a better way: a pulp of tree bark, old rags and fishing nets, spread thin and dried.

Han inventors also made the wheelbarrow, strong iron ploughs and a rudder to steer ships. In AD 132, Zhang Heng made a bronze jar that showed which way an earthquake came from. China kept silk-making secret, so others had to buy its silk.

In 138 BC, Emperor Wu sent Zhang Qian west to find friends against enemies in the north. Zhang Qian was captured and held for about 10 years, escaped, and came home with news of far kingdoms and fine horses. Traders soon followed.

The Silk Road was not one road but many routes. They ran over 6,000 km across deserts and mountains, from the Han capital Chang'an to the Mediterranean Sea. Two-humped camels carried loads, and most traders went only part of the way.

Silk went west, loved by rich Romans. Horses, glass, gold, wool and grapes came east. Ideas travelled too: Buddhism reached China along the routes, and centuries later the art of paper-making went west.
Try it in the world: build a caravan rest house, with stables around a courtyard, on the road between two of your towns, and trade goods there. Next: the Maya.

exercises.prompt: Which dynasty ruled China from 206 BC?
exercises.hint: Many Chinese people still use its name for themselves.
exercises.explain: The Han dynasty, from 206 BC to AD 220.

exercises.prompt: What did Cai Lun show the emperor in AD 105?
exercises.hint: Tree bark, rags and old fishing nets.
choices: a better way to make paper
exercises.explain: A better way to make paper, from a pulp of bark, rags and nets.

exercises.prompt: The Silk Road was one straight road.
exercises.hint: Think of deserts and mountains in the way.
exercises.explain: False: it was many routes across deserts and mountains.

exercises.prompt: Which animal carried loads across the Silk Road's deserts?
exercises.hint: It can go a long time without water.
exercises.explain: The two-humped camel: it stores fat and walks well in cold, dry deserts.

exercises.prompt: Silk went west to Rome along the Silk Road.
exercises.hint: What did rich Romans love to wear?
exercises.explain: True: Chinese silk reached Rome, passed from trader to trader.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: went west from China, or came east to China?
exercises.hint: China made silk and paper; what did it want from the west?
exercises.explain: West: silk, and later paper-making. East: horses, glass, grapes and Buddhism.

exercises.prompt: Match each person to what they did.
exercises.hint: One was a traveller, one an official, one an inventor, one an emperor.
exercises.explain: Zhang Qian travelled west, Cai Lun improved paper, Zhang Heng made the earthquake jar and Liu Bang founded the Han.

exercises.prompt: Why did most traders go only part of the way?
exercises.hint: Over 6,000 km of deserts and mountains.
choices: the whole way was very long and hard
the emperor did not allow it
exercises.explain: The routes were very long and hard, so goods were sold on from trader to trader.

exercises.prompt: What did the Chinese write on before paper?
exercises.hint: One grew in forests, one came from silkworms.

exercises.prompt: Zhang Heng's bronze jar showed which direction an earthquake came from.
exercises.explain: True: made in AD 132, it showed the direction of an earthquake.

exercises.prompt: The Han dynasty began in 206 BC and ended in AD 220. How many years is that? Remember: there is no year 0.
exercises.hint: Count the years up to AD 1, then the years after it.
exercises.explain: From 206 BC to AD 1 is 206 years; from AD 1 to AD 220 is 219 more. 206 + 219 = 425 years.

exercises.prompt: Why was paper such an important invention?
exercises.hint: Compare it with heavy bamboo strips and costly silk.
choices: it was cheap and light to write on
exercises.explain: Paper was cheap, light and easy to make, so more people could write and read.

exercises.prompt: Put Zhang Qian's journey in order.
exercises.hint: He set out in 138 BC and came back years later.
exercises.explain: Sent west, captured, escaped to far kingdoms, then home with news.
Buddhism came from India to China along the Silk Road routes.

exercises.prompt: Why did China keep silk-making secret?
exercises.hint: Who earned money when Romans wanted silk?
choices: so others had to buy Chinese silk
it was not allowed to be sold
exercises.explain: If nobody else could make silk, everyone had to buy it from China.

exercises.prompt: Put these Han times in order, earliest first.
items: Zhang Qian is sent west (138 BC)
exercises.hint: BC dates come before AD dates. With BC, the bigger number is earlier.
exercises.explain: BC counts down, so 206 BC (the Han begin) comes before 138 BC (Zhang Qian). AD counts up, so AD 105 (paper) comes before AD 132 (the earthquake jar).
